name: Estrogen topical for hair
lead: Topical estrogen for hair refers to estrogenic solutions applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss, with the aim of keeping more of the hair a person has so the hairline and crown look fuller for longer. The best-documented example is alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as an ethanol-based scalp solution in Germany and several Latin American countries under names such as Ell-Cranell Alpha, Avicis, Avixis and Pantostin.[1]

Wikipedia describes alfatradiol as used continuously for pattern hair loss in men and women, with limited regrowth of lost hair and poorer response in advanced alopecia.[1] A 1980 randomized double-blind study reported reduced androgenic hair loss without effective new growth, and a 2007 university-led study of 103 women found minoxidil performed better than alfatradiol, which slowed or stabilized loss without increasing hair density or thickness.[1]

Alfatradiol is the 17-alpha stereoisomer of the body's main estrogen, 17-beta-estradiol, and was studied in the 1980s and 2000s as an anti-androgen-style hair treatment, alongside other agents such as minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride and ketoconazole.[1][4] Interest from people dealing with pattern hair loss rests on the idea that a locally acting, weakly estrogenic 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor might lower scalp DHT without the systemic effects of oral drugs.[1][4]

Estrogen is also associated with thicker hair during pregnancy, and estradiol has documented skin effects, but its role as a hair-loss treatment beyond alfatradiol is not established in general medical references.[2][3]

paras: Pattern hair loss is androgen-dependent and genetically influenced. DHT, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, is the main androgen acting on the follicle's dermal papilla, and in scalp follicles androgens appear to push follicles into an early resting phase and shrink them, a process called miniaturisation. Wikipedia notes that miniaturised follicles are probably dormant rather than gone.[4]

About half of men and a quarter of women are affected by age 50, according to Wikipedia. Standard treatments it lists include minoxidil, finasteride (a type II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor), dutasteride (a type I and II inhibitor approved for male pattern hair loss in Korea and Japan), combinations with ketoconazole, hair transplantation, and preliminary options such as low-level laser and platelet-rich plasma.[4] On estrogen, the same article notes that estrogens can increase IGF release, which may support growth.[4]

Alfatradiol is a stereoisomer of 17-beta-estradiol, differing only in the stereochemistry at carbon 17. It binds estrogen receptors with much lower activity, and is described as having roughly 100-fold lower estrogenic activity, and it inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.[1] Dihydrotestosterone is the hormone implicated in androgenetic hair loss.[2]

17-alpha-estradiol binds ER-alpha and ER-beta with about 58 and 11 percent of estradiol's affinity, does not meaningfully bind the membrane receptor GPER, and binds the brain-expressed ER-X receptor more potently than estradiol. In rats its uterus-growing effect is far weaker than estradiol's.[1] Wikipedia notes that comparison tables in the article give inconsistent binding values, so the figures are approximate.[1]

Alfatradiol is applied to the scalp as an ethanolic solution and must be used continuously to keep preventing further hair loss, according to Wikipedia; regrowth of lost hair is limited, and advanced alopecia generally responds poorly to treatment.[1] For comparison, Wikipedia's androgenetic alopecia article describes minoxidil as the best-supported treatment for female pattern hair loss.[4]
Wikipedia also attributes alfatradiol's limited regrowth in advanced alopecia to the loss of hair roots, and lists ketoconazole, finasteride and dutasteride among other hair-loss drugs.[1]

Local burning or itching, attributed to the ethanol vehicle, and increased sebum production are reported for alfatradiol; its leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under age 18 [1]. Estradiol more broadly is associated with clotting and hormone-sensitive cancer risks in general discussions, though these are described for estrogen use overall rather than topical scalp products specifically [3].

17-alpha-estradiol is a minor component (under 10 percent) of conjugated estrogens such as Premarin, used in men and women since the 1930s, where it is present as a sulfated sodium salt.[1] Milestones noted by Wikipedia include the 1980 hair-loss trial, a 2005 neuroprotection study, the 2007 minoxidil comparison and a 2009 review of human studies.[1] Several authors of the 2007 comparison advised companies including Pfizer.[1]

Alfatradiol is sold as a scalp solution in Germany and several Latin American countries including Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, and is listed as prescription-only in the US.[1] On T Nation, hair loss on testosterone therapy and anabolic steroids is a frequent topic, and posters debate which topical anti-androgens are acceptable: one reply argued that topical ketoconazole and spironolactone appear to have little systemic absorption, in response to another poster who equated them with taking estrogen.[5]
Alfatradiol has also been studied for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and a 2017 mouse study reported improved insulin resistance and metabolic function without feminisation.[1]

A 1980 randomized, double-blind study of alfatradiol (Orfanos and Vogels) reported no systemic side effects and a reduction in androgenic hair loss, but no effective new hair growth.[1] A 2007 university-led study of 103 women (Blume-Peytavi et al.) compared it with minoxidil: minoxidil performed better, while alfatradiol slowed or stabilised hair loss without increasing density or thickness.[1] No studies were found of topical 17-beta-estradiol or other estrogen preparations specifically for hair loss.

lore.intro: Topical estrogen is rarely discussed directly in forum material; hair-loss conversation on T Nation centres on managing hair on testosterone and steroids, where concerns about estrogenic and anti-androgen topicals arise.[5]

claims.claim: Topical anti-androgens and estrogen-like solutions act only locally
claims.believers: One T Nation poster argued that topical ketoconazole and spironolactone don't appear to have significant systemic absorption and that minoxidil has no hormonal side effects.[5]
claims.experts: For alfatradiol, Wikipedia reports no systemic side effects in the 1980 randomized study; the package leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 because safety is unknown.[1]

claims.believers: Some products are marketed in Germany and Latin America as hair-loss treatments.[1]
claims.experts: The 1980 study found reduced loss but no effective new growth, and the 2007 study of 103 women found alfatradiol slowed or stabilised loss without increasing density or thickness, with minoxidil performing better.[1]

card.summary: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, that may slow thinning in some regions but are not shown to regrow hair.
card.note: Not widely approved; label advises against use in pregnancy and under 18.

quick.overview:
Topical estrogen for hair usually means alfatradiol, a weak estrogen scalp solution sold in some countries for pattern hair loss.

Reports describe it slowing or stabilizing loss rather than thickening hair, and minoxidil outperformed it in a women's study.
quick.mechanism: Alfatradiol binds estrogen receptors weakly and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT.
quick.risks: Scalp irritation from the alcohol vehicle and more oil production are reported. Safety in pregnancy and minors is unknown.

chain: Weak estrogen solution applied to the scalp
Hair loss slowed or stabilised, so more existing hair is kept
angle.text: Alfatradiol is applied to the scalp to slow androgen-driven thinning, so existing hair is retained rather than lost. In the studies described, it stabilised loss more than it thickened hair.
